---
title: "The decision for an isolated pair"
subtitle: "2.1 · after the postrank theory book, ch. 10, and Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), slides 18–20"
description: "Posterior expected loss of the two strict directions and withholding for a single pair."
---

For an isolated pair, the action with the smallest posterior expected loss depends on the direction probability and
the cost of withholding. The two strict directions incur their respective error probabilities; withholding incurs
a fixed cost τ. The graph expresses these losses as functions of $e_{AB}=1-\pi_{AB}$, the probability that stating
A above B is wrong. An increase in $\pi_{AB}$ therefore moves the selected pair to the **left**. The horizontal
withholding line and the two directional lines identify the loss-minimising actions, including ties at their
intersections.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **π .85, τ .10.** Stating A above B is wrong with probability .15, above the .10 cost of withholding, which minimises loss.
  The grey dot marks this minimum despite the posterior support for A above B. Its height varies with the withholding cost.
- **π .85, τ .20.** The posterior is unchanged, but the withholding cost increases. The error remains .15, below .20, so the selected action is “state A above B”.
  Only the horizontal line moved; the posterior probability and both directional costs stayed fixed.
- **π .80, τ .20.** The error equals .20: stating A above B and withholding have equal expected loss, labelled “equally good”. The open circle marks
  their crossing, and both dots receive a ring. A ring identifies a minimum-cost action at the current pair; it does not
  identify a correct direction in the unknown truth.
- **π .50, τ .50.** Both directions cost .50 and withholding also costs .50; the summary reads “all three actions are equally good”.
  The crossing circles merge, while the table marks every action as minimum-cost.

The shaded area follows the smallest cost along the whole error axis. The scale above the graph connects a
direction probability to its error, and the table beside it gives the costs at the selected pair.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
This example gives equal true values probability zero. For an isolated pair, disclose only when the posterior
probability of the direction exceeds $1-\tau$; at equality, disclosing and withholding tie. A shared grade withholds a
direction rather than asserting equal true values. Combining many pair decisions into one coherent report adds a
constraint that this isolated-pair rule does not impose.
:::

Standalone: [embed/one-pair.html](../../embed/one-pair.html), for example `?pi=.9&tau=.05` or
